articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery is inviting the community to join for the 17th Annual Tulip Exhibition at the cemetery’s Tower Chapel this Friday-Sunday, March 21-23, 10:00 a.m.-4:00 p.m. The free event welcomes in Spring with a showing of blooming Dutch tulips and striking floral arrangements by Bay Area florists, garden clubs and students from college floral design class. “Tulip Magic” by Phoebe Kahl and Nancy Huseby “Tulips and Dots in Motion” by Agnes Kang Photos by Matt Simons Since its inception in 2006, the cemetery’s annual tulip exhibit has become a cherished community tradition. Under the guidance of Special Events Coordinator Kristie Ly, this year is the exhibit’s second year back after a hiatus due to COVID-19 restrictions. “We have some new artists joining us this year… it’ll be a nice surprise to see what they come up with this year,” said Ly. Following the exhibition, attendees may enjoy a Pop-up Arts Show at J. Miller Flowers one block away, in honor of the store’s 55th Anniversary. Mountain View Cemetery (5000 Piedmont Avenue) is an historic garden cemetery in the foothills of Oakland and Piedmont. One of the oldest cemeteries in the Western U.S., it has served the community since 1863 and even includes a section for Civil War soldiers. For more information on the cemetery or its annual tulip exhibition, visit www.mountainviewcemetery.org.

articles.text: Editor: On February 23, Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan delivered a presentation about wildfire preparedness at an event sponsored by the League of Women Voters. One of the things he mentioned is that the Fire Department has three individuals who can inspect Piedmonters’ homes and offer recommendations about hardening against wildfires. A couple of weeks later I called to request an inspection. This past weekend, Captain Mike Carlisle, accompanied by two firefighters, came to our house. Much of what we discussed was information that I already knew (and that I appreciated having reinforced). However, Mike made a point that I was aware of but whose significance I had not fully appreciated and personalized. That point: If we are subjected to a wildfire, it will be driven by hot, dry winds coming downhill from the east. This means that the side of the house that deserves the greatest attention is the east side. In our case, that is the front, so that is where I will be paying the greatest attention in the near term. Driving around Piedmont, it appears that no one has a fire-hardened house – we all have vegetation coming up to, often right against, our exterior walls. I urge all Piedmonters to call the Fire Department to arrange an inspection and to start protecting their homes, as well as the homes of their neighbors. –Dana H. articles.text: A view of parking on Vista Avenue by the tennis courts. Piedmont City Council held a discussion on public parking in Piedmont’s Civic Center at their meeting on Monday, March 17, to look into how to best balance competing demands for parking in the constrained area. The presentation included results from a parking survey with over 500 respondents on parking in the Civic Center area, where roughly half of respondents reported that they found parking in the area either “somewhat” or “very” difficult. “One thing is very obvious – we have limited parking and many, many points of view on how parking should be assigned,” said City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore while introducing the discussion topic. “This isn’t an easy topic to arrive at a conclusion, but the good news is we’re just at the beginning so it’s a great time to collect input.” As a starting point, City staff presented a “maximum” parking scenario, which demonstrates what it would look like to restripe the Civic Center to provide the largest amount of public parking spaces. This maximum scenario would bring the current 233 parking spaces in the area up to 396 spaces if implemented as-is. This scenario was presented primarily to provide a starting point for discussion, and no actions were taken at the meeting. The “maximum” scenario includes converting 16 formerly temporary spaces near the Sheridan strip to permanent spaces and converting Bonita between Vista and Oakland Avenues into a one-way street with diagonal parking on one side. The scenario Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales (left) presents a parking scenario to the City Council. does not consider any changes to residential permit parking in the Civic Center. This discussion follows several years of disruption to historical parking distribution in the Civic Center area, beginning with the construction of the new STEAM building and theater on the Piedmont High School campus, when “Permit A” restrictions were added to existing parking spaces along Magnolia. An additional 57 spaces were lost in 2023 when construction began on the new community pool. Further spaces were removed or redesignated in summer 2024 to accommodate construction on the Police Department’s new 9-1-1 dispatch center. Topics for further discussion include designated parking for City employees and PUSD teachers, pick-up and drop-off zones, and permitted parking. Some discussion was also given to parking enforcement, including the possibility of raising ticket charges as a deterrent for parking violations. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales noted community concerns his department received in regard to parking, including safety concerns for vehicles reversing from driveways, pedestrian traffic, and Fire Department access. In response, Gonzales stated that one way streets (as Bonita would become in the maximum parking plan) are generally safer, and that additional parking would be likely to act as a traffic calming element by narrowing the roadway. articles.text: Piper, a 2-year-old, 41-pound bundle of fun, was having quite an adventure on the streets of Oakland before being scooped up by a kind stranger who is now her foster. Since then, Piper has been soaking up the good life in a home with three much larger doggy roommates, proving she’s as playful as she is adaptable. Piper is a smart, spunky, and affectionate girl who loves playing just as much as she loves snuggling up with her humans. She’s always ready for a game of chase or a romp in the yard, but when bedtime rolls around, she sprints to her crate and sleeps soundly all night long. According to her foster, Piper is a great mix of fun, feisty, and affectionate. She adores car rides, hikes, belly rubs, and sunbathing. If you’re looking for a playful, active, and loyal companion, Come meet Piper at Oakland Animal Services. Piper can’t wait to meet you! To meet Piper, go on the Oakland Animal Services website and fill out an adoption questionnaire which will be sent to her foster who will contact you to arrange a time for a meet and greet. For more information, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@gmail.com. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Millennium High School Principal Irma Muñoz Daniels provided a report to the school board during its February 26 meeting on the breadth of the work at the school district’s Wellness Center. The Wellness Center provides free and confidential counseling on-campus; the report also provided historical data on usage and financials for the Center. Muñoz Daniels is also the administrator of Wellness Center, whose staff include Nurses Claudia Garcia and Carol Menz, Health Clerk Maddy Sage, and Clinical Supervisors Alisa Crovetti and Sari Sanghvi. The Center is also supported by trainees and interns from Berkeley Psychology Internship Consortium. The Wellness Center, started in 2007 by Piedmont Middle School’s Brooke Zimmerman, offers students at PHS, MHS and PMS drop-in sessions for: academic stress, social-emotional stress, parent/child communication, peer relationships, sexual orientation/gender questions, anxiety and depression, grief and loss, substance abuse, resiliency and self-advocacy. In addition to drop-in appointments the Wellness Center offers short-term weekly sessions, crisis intervention and one-on-one ongoing counseling through the school year. “I think it’s important to call out how efficient a model it is, the number of hours of service we are able to provide for our kids for a relatively low dollar amount is pretty incredible,” said School Board President Lindsay Thomasson. The most reported reason for going to the Wellness Center is for stress or anxiety, with 70% of all visitors. Managing stressors such as loss or family dynamics accounts for 10% of visits, 5% report depression or lack of motivation and another 5% visit for social issues. articles.text: Spring is the poster month for observation – a basic part of the scientific process. As sunlight shifts, we are acutely aware of changes in weather, the appearance of wildflowers, seasonal local produce, new baby wildlife, the return of migratory birds and that just plain “feels-good-to-bealive” sensation. We are tempted and inspired to get up and out to check out what’s going on now that the rains and cooler weather are retreating. This inspiration, curiosity and observation of the natural world around us makes each of us a scientist. We pay attention, take mental note of changes and think about what causes them and what they may mean. We have expectations of what will happen based on our observations of springtimes past and notice if the poppies are early or late and wonder if we’ll get a superbloom this year. We remark to friends or family that we should take a hike to that overlook with a spectacular view that is always so memorable and green this time of year. Some of us go deeper and look up what we see and experience online or in guidebooks/ We might even ask a naturalist or guide at t local park or nature center. Some take field notes or write in nature journals. We encourage younger people or invite elders to join us or even just spark a conversation by remarking on how beautiful the wild irises are or how have you notice how many pesky geese there are at Lake Merritt. Following your heart and following the seasons by observing changes and things around you that interest and engage a sense of wonder is a great way to learn about nature and hone some personal skills as an everyday scientist. Here are a few great ways to observe and learn more this spring; check out nature guides at your local library or bookstore. articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation’s (PEF) Spring Fling season, Palm Royale, is dedicated to the “A” in STEAM, the arts. Enhancements to the visual and performing arts programs at Beach, Havens and Wildwood are on the horizon and can be supported through the Palm Royale April 25 event. Piedmont children deserve to learn with musical instruments and art supplies in good repair. As fourth and fifth graders look forward to music theory and learning string instruments, Spring Fling will ensure they have sheet music and enough violins. Funds raised also will go toward supplying arts and crafts rooms, upgrading theater performances and setting up instrument repair funds for all grades. The ability to purchase classroom enhancements, large and small, outside of Piedmont Unified School District’s (PUSD) budgeted expenditures is what sets the Spring Fling season apart from the Giving Campaign. Funds raised through the Giving Campaign are used to supplement PUSD’s budget needs. “Parent contributions through the annual Giving Campaign help close the gap between what PUSD receives from government funds and what it actually costs to provide each student with an excellent education,” said PEF Executive Director Heather Frank. Funds raised through the Spring Fling season are supplemental to the PUSD budget. Last year, the Spring Fling season funded decodable books to enhance student literacy, classroom technology to build computer skills and a contract with Playworks to promote a positive playground experience. This year, elementary parents have the opportunity to help build an expanded program for visual and performing arts. “Children love visual and performing arts in our elementary schools, and expanding these programs will provide an amazing opportunity for them to develop creativity and self-expression skills,” said Spring Fling Co-Chair Monika Riddle. Parents also will have the opportunity to “raise the paddle,” either at the gala or on PiedmontSpringFling.org, to continue the investment in elementary counseling at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood. Tickets and sponsorship opportunities for the April 25 Palm Royale Gala are available online. Piedmont students take part in an Improv class at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse.
articles.title: Spring Fling’s Palm Royale raises funds for the arts

Enhancements to the visual and performing arts programs at Beach, Havens and Wildwood are on the horizon and can be supported through the Palm Royale April 25 event. Piedmont children deserve to learn with musical instruments and art supplies in good repair. As fourth and fifth graders look forward to music theory and learning string instruments, Spring Fling will ensure they have sheet music and enough violins. Funds raised also will go toward supplying arts and crafts rooms, upgrading theater performances and setting up instrument repair funds for all grades. The ability to purchase classroom enhancements, large and small, outside of Piedmont Unified School District’s (PUSD) budgeted expenditures is what sets the Spring Fling season apart from the Giving Campaign. Funds raised through the Giving Campaign are used to supplement PUSD’s budget needs. “Parent contributions through the annual Giving Campaign help close the gap between what PUSD receives from government funds and what it actually costs to provide each student with an excellent education,” said PEF Executive Director Heather Frank. Funds raised through the Spring Fling season are supplemental to the PUSD budget. Last year, the Spring Fling season funded decodable books to enhance student literacy, classroom technology to build computer skills and a contract with Playworks to promote a positive playground experience. This year, elementary parents have the opportunity to help build an expanded program for visual and performing arts. “Children love visual and performing arts in our elementary schools, and expanding these programs will provide an amazing opportunity for them to develop creativity and self-expression skills,” said Spring Fling Co-Chair Monika Riddle. Parents also will have the opportunity to “raise the paddle,” either at the gala or on PiedmontSpringFling.org, to continue the investment in elementary counseling at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood. Tickets and sponsorship opportunities for the April 25 Palm Royale Gala are available online. articles.text: The Piedmont High School College and Career Center hosted a Young Alumni Career Panel on February 27, in conjunction with the Career Exploration Day at PHS and a resume writing workshop. Principal David Yoshihara led the panel discussion in the Alan Harvey Theater with recent Piedmont High School (PHS) alums Frannie Lahey-Teare, Jordan Marcus, and Sara Siqueira. “I think being really comfortable asking questions and asking for help is something I had to practice and learn. It’s scary sometimes,” said Siqueira as advice upon starting a new job. Frannie Lahey-Teare, PHS graduate of 2019, took a gap Panel members, students and parents are shown in Alan Harvey Theater after the panel talk. Photos by Linda Song Wendel Frannie Lahey-Teare (left), Jordan Marcus, and Sara Siqueira on stage Jordan Marcus (left), Sara Siqueira, Frannie Lahey-Teare with PHS Judy Lin (left) and Kim Hunter (right) work one-on-one with students at the Resume Writing Workshop. year, before going to University of Denver. She is currently an immigration paralegal and plans to take the LSAT exam this year. Jordan Marcus graduated from Piedmont in 2017 and from the University of Michigan in 2020. Marcus works for Pilot, an accounting startup in San Francisco, in the sales department. Marcus, who transferred to Piedmont for high school, reflected on the benefits of being on the debate team at PHS. Sara Siqueira graduated from PHS in 2018 and studied Cognitive Science at Tufts College. She now works in San Francisco with Niantic, the developer of Pokémon Go. She reflected on enjoying her time writing for The Piedmont Highlander while in high school and the lasting relationships she made from Piedmont Choirs. Yoshihara asked the panel questions that included, “What were you like in high school?” “If you could go back to high school what one thing would you do differently?” “What do you enjoy most about your job and what do you find less appealing?” The young professional alumni forum included food and a meet and greet reception in the Alan Harvey foyer. The career-focused events at PHS were organized by parents Alder Yarrow, Kim Hunter, Linda Song Wendel, Sara Ironside and Judy Lin. In addition to Career Exploration Day, and the Young Professionals forum there was a resume writing workshop on Friday, February 28.

Several citizens spoke during public comment, urging the Council to consider the safety of student pedestrians and consider conducting further analysis on traffic safety before moving forward with any changes. Marcia Lane, a Community Pool Advisory Committee member, made special note that 43 parking spaces would be returned upon completion of pool construction. “Should we not gain those spots back and see what happens before we make major structural changes to the center of town?” asked Lane at the discussion. A potentially key topic in the discussion was the importance of parking for businesses in the area, especially looking toward the eventual completion of the community pool project. Customers and pool-goers need space to park during their visits, pointing toward a future discussion of 30-minute, 2-hour or 4-hour spaces, including how many of each and where. Jon Sakol, Piedmont resident for 48 years and one of the designers of the previous pool revenue model, stressed the importance of parking if the City hopes to generate revenue to maintain the pool. “If, when the pool opens, the impression is ‘good facility, no parking’, we’ll spend years trying to overcome that,” said Sakol. Civic Center parking will return again as a discussion topic at a future City Council meeting, sometime in April or May. Residents can contact Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales (dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov) for more information as discussion continues. articles.text: Jenelle Solis named Co-Player of the Year Winter sports has come and gone. Each of Piedmont High’s four varsity teams reached the North Coast Section post-season playoffs. The boys’ soccer, boys’ basketball and girls’ basketball teams qualified for the CIF State tournaments. BOYS’ SOCCER Newman in the opening round on February 20, while they won 70-48 over No. 6 Salesian in the fifth-place final on February 26. Being in the Open Division earned them an automatic berth into the CIF State Tournament, receiving the No. 9 seed in the Division 1 bracket for the second-straight year. They beat No. 8 Oakland Tech 60-29 in the first round on March 4 and No. 16 San Joaquin Memorial 62-60 two days later. They lost to No. 4 St. Mary’s of Stockton 61-48 on March 8. Jenelle Solis, a freshman, was named the WACC Co-Player of the Year. The boys soccer team finished 13-4-9 (W-T-L) overall, reaching the Division 4 NCS Final as the No. 1 seed. They won Div. 5 CIF NorCal tournament as the No. 5 seed. In North Coast Section, PHS beat No. 16 Justin-Siena 2-0 the opening round on February 19, won 4-2 over No. 9 Urban in the quarterfinals on February 22, won 2-0 over No. 4 San Rafael in semifinals four days, but lost to No. 2 Roseland University Prep 2-0 in the Final on March 1. After qualifying for the CIF NorCal tournament, Piedmont beat No. 4 Orland 1-0 to start on March 4, won 2-0 over No. 8 Colusa in the semifinals two days later, and defeated No. 7 Williams 4-1 for the championship on March 8. BOYS’ BASKETBALL The Highlanders went 15-16 and reached the D4 NCS Finals as the No. 1 seed before losing No. 11 St. Patrick 75-70 on March 1. To get there, PHS beat No. 16 Ukiah 87-49 in the first round on February 19, No. 9 Bethel 78-69 in the quarterfinals on February 22 and No. 12 Windsor 60-53 in the semifinals on February 26. They qualified for the D4 CIF State tournament as the No. 9 seed, losing to No. 8 Natomas 84-71 on March 4. The girls’ basketball team had seven All-League selections: Briana Webb (left), Jenelle Solis, Cleo Afsar, Andrea Martin, Shakila Zuberi, Taylor White, and Savannah Dennig. GIRLS’ BASKETBALL GIRLS’ SOCCER The girls’ basketball team finished with a 25-6 overall record and was co-WACC Champions alongside Bishop O’Dowd, marking the school’s third consecutive WACC banner. They received the No. 5 seed in the NCS Open Division, which is considered the upper echelon of the section. They lost 51-45 to No. 4 Cardinal The girls’ soccer team finished with a 7-2-10 (W-T-L) overall record and earned the No. 1 seed in the D4 NCS bracket. They demolished No. 16 College Prep 5-1 in the opening round on February 19 but fell 2-0 to No. 8 Pinole Valley in the quarterfinals on February 22. The girls’ soccer team earned eight All-League selections: Ava Sauer (left), Eliza Hammond, Louisa Symkowick, Juliana Thornborrow, Ryo Woltag, and Kyra Trombi. articles.text: PHS fall to Las Lomas 8-7 in double OT Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team suffered a pair of losses over the past week. They took a one-sided 18-6 loss against North Coast Section foe Branson at Witter Field on Tuesday, March 11. Three days later they battled to an 8-7 loss in double overtime against Las Lomas in Walnut Creek. Las Lomas is a Division 1 North Coast Section opponent, while Piedmont plays in Division 2. “We were up with about 14 seconds left against Las Lomas and just could not hold them. It was really a tough loss,” coach Carlton Chan said. Branson looks like a top team in Div. 2 North Coast Section and currently is undefeated at 4-0. “The Branson girls are very good. We had a 3rd quarter “comeback” where we were just scoring and reducing their lead. We just ran out of gas.” said Chan. Piedmont visits Northgate in Walnut Creek on March 20 and returns home on March 25 against Dublin. Both teams are in Division 1. 8-7 to Las Lomas in Double OT Piedmont held a 2-1 lead through the first quarter and extended the lead to 5-3 by halftime. However, Piedmont could only muster two goals in the second half, while Las Lomas scored the tying goal with just 12 seconds left in the fourth. In the first quarter, Friedie Schickedanz scored the game’s opening goal at the 10:50 mark, but Las Lomas answered on the next possession just 20 seconds later. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team suffered a 12-8 loss to North Coast Section foe Casa Grande in Petaluma on Tuesday, March 11. The game brought together Casa Gande head coach and former Piedmont assistant Matt Palasek with new Piedmont head coach Paul Pappas and his assistant, Georgie Brayer. Palasek, who coached at Piedmont from 2021-2023, has provided his team two emblems to wear on helmets, numbers 1 and 16 to honor former players he coached in Piedmont, Jack Nelson and Soren Dixon who died in an auto accident last November, Piedmont High will officially retire Nelson and Dixon’s numbers on March 28. Piedmont went into halftime trailing 9-0 to the Gauchos, but stormed back in the second half, holding them scoreless in the fourth quarter. The result brings PHS’ record to 2-2. It was a strong game for Timmy Kalamas and Ian Nguyen who each had a 3-goal hat trick Goalie Gus Von Metzsch had a busy night, recording 13 saves. 12-8 loss to Casa Grande Casa Grande scored five goals in the first quarter and added another four in the second to take a commanding 9-0 lead. In the third quarter, Casa Grande added one more goal to make it 10-0 with seven minutes left. Piedmont then got on the board when Timmy Kalamas scored with 4:54 on the clock, but Casa Grande netted another on its next possession. Connor Fredericks then scored with 40 seconds left, but the Gauchos scored its final goals with 11 seconds left— making it 12-2 to start the fourth, and the comeback was on. Photos by JC Curran Piedmont head coach Paul Pappas (right) and assistant coach Georgie Brayer (left) with Casa Grande head coach and former PHS assistant Matt Palasek. Ian Ngueyn had three goals and four ground balls.

articles.text: The Piedmont High School swim team made waves at the De La Salle Invitational, competing with 25 schools and nearly 700 athletes in one of the most anticipated early-season meets. With 16 swimmers representing Piedmont, the team delivered an impressive performance, with the boys finishing fifth overall and the girls placing 12th. Head coach Adrien Downey emphasized the significance of the De La Salle Invitational, calling it an opportunity to race toptier competition in a high-level setting without the pressure of a championship meet. “It’s a chance to test ourselves against strong teams and see where we stand early in the season,” Downey said. Among the highlights, Abigail Jacoby excelled for the girls’ team, contributing to all of their points across two relay events and two individual races — the 200 individual medley (IM) and the 500 freestyle. “That’s a rare feat,” Downey noted. “Her consistency across both Friday preliminaries and Saturday finals was incredible.” Freshman Charlotte Zhang also made an impact in her varsity debut, posting strong relay performances. On the boys’ side, Piedmont focused on strengthening their relays, a strategy that paid off with a third-place finish in the 200 medley relay final. “That was probably our best-executed race of the meet,” Downey said. Dima Secor and Cole Carnazzo made their mark in the 200 IM, becoming the only Piedmont swimmers to qualify for the A final in the same event. Several swimmers punched their tickets to the North Coast Section (NCS) championships with automatic qualifying times. All three boys’ relays earned NCS auto times, along with individual cuts for Secor (200 IM, 100 freestyle) and Carnazzo (200 IM, 100 breaststroke). “It’s a relief and a confidence boost for them, especially given how hard they are training right now,” said Downey. “They will be even faster soon.” Additionally, Piedmont swimmers set new school records. The boys’ 200 medley relay team of Asher Takazawa, Cole Carnazzo, Owen Blanford and Nik Costello shattered the previous school record by several seconds with a time of 1:35.18. Secor and Carnazzo also broke their own school records in the 200 IM and 100 breaststroke, respectively. With the meet behind them, the team now shifts its focus back to dual meet competition, starting with a matchup against Arroyo on Friday. articles.text: After witnessing the horrific firestorm in January which ravaged areas of Los Angeles, particularly in the Pacific Palisades area, everyone immediately thought of all the families and their children. The statistics behind girls leaving athletics in high school are known and alarming. Entering my 9th year at PHS as an assistant coach, I have always been focused on female interest in and retention on our cross country/track teams and losing everything in an instant would certainly be a reason to quit. What could we do to support our sisters in sport? This is where TeamUp was born. We were going to rally to team up to support the girls at Palisades Charter High School. A division 1 team within the LA City Section, their school was damaged in the fire to the extent all instruction was moved online and the scramble to find athletic venues began. Through their school website and Facebook messenger, I was able to contact their head track coach, Claudius Shropshire to ask about his athletes. Twenty girls on his team either lost their entire homes or were displaced to find new homes. Practices were moved to a city college an hour drive each way. I floated the idea of a gently used running apparel drive to our girls’ team’s parents; everyone loved it and went into action. In the first week of practice in February sixteen current girl track athletes went into their closet and delivered. The statistics behind girls leaving athletics in high school are known and alarming. Entering my 9th year at PHS as an assistant coach, I have always been focused on female interest in and retention on our cross country/track teams and losing everything in an instant would certainly be a reason to quit. articles.text: Mathias Kauage at Ray Hughes Gallery February 1999. A rare and unique exhibition featuring artwork by contemporary Papuan artist Mathias Kauage is on display at the de Young Museum in San Francisco, now through March 2026. Kauage is regarded as the leading figure of contemporary art in Papua New Guinea and exhibited internationally in Europe, America and Australia regularly before he died in 2003. The exhibition features four paintings from the de Young’s permanent collection by Mathias Kauage and his family, on view for the first time. Born in 1944 in a remote village in Papua New Guinea’s remote highlands, the artist moved to Port Moreseby, the country’s capital, as a teenager. He began drawing at a young age when he was inspired by the work of Timothy Akis, the first Papuan artist to hold a western-style exhibition. Under the mentorship Photo by Gary Sexton Installation view of Contemporary Painting in Papua New Guinea: Mathias Kauage and His Family Photo by Ben Rushton of German artist Gerogina Beier at the National Arts School in Port Moresby, Kauage began to develop his own distinctive style and find his preferred medium of acrylic on canvas. He also learned and mastered printmaking techniques, woodcuts and copper-beating. Kauage is most famous for his acrylic on canvas paintings and murals, which are highlighted in this exhibit. His works famously focused on how technology has impacted life in remote Papua New Guinea, and his later works addressed societal issues such as the onset of the HIV/AIDS epidemic. In the late 1970s, Kauage and his wife Elisabet led the contemporary arts movement in the newly independent Papua New Guinea. His works are currently held in the National Gallery of Australia, the National Gallery of Papua New Guinea, the British Museum and the Gallery of Modern Art, Glasgow, but are less often on display in Western museums, making the de Young’s exhibition a rarity. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/papua-new-guinea-mathias-kauage. articles.text: Sona Jobarteh Gambian multi-instrumentalist, singer and composer Sona Jobarteh performs at the Herbst Theatre in San Francisco Friday, April 4. Called “A griot for a new generation of West Africans” by BBC Radio, Jobarteh is regarded as a master and a pioneer of the kora, a unique 21-string African lute. Most similar to a lute or a harp, the kora is played almost exclusively in West Africa and was first discovered in the Gambia. Music for the kora was not written until the 20th century. Songs are passed down from griots, composed of West African storytellers, singers, musicians, and oral historians. Griots also keep records of all births, deaths, marriages through the generations of the village and pass traditionally composed music down to younger generations. Gambian griot traditions date back nearly seven centuries. Jobarteh, born in London, is from one of only five principal kora-playing ‘griot’ families of West Africa and is the first female professional kora player to come from a griot family. She is the granddaughter of the griot of her line, Amadu Bansang Jobarteh, whose father migrated from Mali to Gambia. Jobarteh’s cousin is celebrated kora player Toumani Diabaté and her brother Tunde Jegede is also a renowned diaspora kora player. Jobar teh’s debut album Afro-Acoustic Soul, released in 2008, is influenced heavily by her Gambian background but also includes melodies that could be heard on more conventional European radio stations. Her second album and first solo recording Fasiya, released in 2011, highlighted her skills as a vocalist and multi-instrumentalist. She returns to SF JAZZ next month following the release of her 2022 follow-up for African Guild Records, Badinyaa Kumoo. Jobarteh performs at the Herbst Theatre, an auditorium in the War Memorial and Performing Arts Center in San Francisco’s Civic Center, on Friday, April 4. articles.text: Marin Theatre play opens tomorrow, March 20 Mrs. Krishnan’s Party, a New Zealand-based company India Ink Theatre Company production by Jacob Rajan and Justin Lewis, opens on the Marin Theatre stage tomorrow, Thursday, March 20. The well-received comedy is an ‘interactive play’ for all ages. Young children aged 8 and under will especially enjoy the play’s fun, party-like atmosphere, and guests are invited to choose from four seating types depending on how much you want to be involved in the action. The play opens with the evening’s host who leads you to your seat and introduces you to audience members in your seating area. Actors are celebrating the Hindu festival of Onam, which marks King Mahabali’s annual visit to Kerala and includes traditional prayers, vibrant decorations, cultural dishes, dance and boat races. Audiences are taken to ‘the back room’ of titular character Mrs. Krishnan’s Dairy Day bodega, the New Zealand equivalent of a convenience store. Guests learn that the host is a college student who is renting a room in the building and has decided to hold a party without telling Mrs. Krishnan. What ensues next depends heavily on the audience, but is sure to include the play’s central theme of renewal and camaraderie that crosses cultural and political borders. Co-playwright Justin Lewis described Onam as “a harvest festival, a time of renewal, and what’s remarkable about that festival is that it’s celebrated by all the different religions in Kerala.” “So, the Christians, the Hindus, the Muslims, everybody celebrates it, and it really brings everybody together. And that’s a lot of what the inspiration for the show is about, it is about connecting people, art, building community, and having a joyous celebration,” he said. Upon its release, New Zealand’s Waikato Times hailed Mrs. Krishnan’s Party as “So different, so original, so creatively fresh, and so much fun no one wanted to go home,” while the New Zealand Herald lauded “the show’s generous spirit [which] offers a timely reminder that live theatre is a gift.” Mrs. Krishnan’s Party plays on the Marin Theatre stage through March 30. articles.text: Shotgun Players in Berkeley launched its 33rd season with Yasmina Reza’s internationally acclaimed Art, playing onstage now through April 6. Art explores dy namics between lifelong friends Serge, Marc, and Yvan as their relationships slowly unravel when Serge, played by Benoît Monin, purchases a $200,000 piece of modern art. Marc, played by David Sinaiko, questions his friend’s extravagant purchase, likening it to a mid-life crisis, while neutral Yvan attempts to mediate arguments between them. The comedy centers on the common adage ‘art is in the eye of the beholder’ but focuses more heavily on the three men’s complex friendships. Eventually, the painting begins to symbolize Serge, Marc, and Yvan’s own perceived failures. “That painting is the first crack for the wall to come tumbling down,” Director Emilie Whelan said of Reza’s play. “[Reza] bears these cracks in the wall [and] lines in the canvas through a mad hilarity. articles.text: Richard Gere and Hilary Swank in Amelia Amelia Earhart vanished over the Pacific Ocean on July 2, 1937. She was attempting to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, something that had never been done before. Her success depended not only on her flying skills but on the ability of Fred Noonan, her navigator. On the Pacific leg of the flight, he would have to find a mere speck of land, Howland Island, in a body of water so vast that there would be no second chance. Told that it was dangerous, perhaps reckless in the extreme – there was a good chance she would run out of fuel – Earhart was committed to trying. She left Miami on June 1 and began what would be her final journey. Earhart was driven to fly, consumed with an unrelenting passion to be in the air, no matter the craft or the challenge. She broke records, flew solo across the Atlantic in a gorgeous, red Lockheed Vega 58, landing to her surprise in Ireland. Amelia attempts to capture the aviatrix’s passion for flight, an unrelenting need to be aloft. It was a desire since childhood to pilot airplanes, and explore the serenity she found aloft which was, in contrast, to the discomfort she often found on land where she became a highly commercialized heroine, her popularity not always of her choosing. Actions could include strengthening building codes, starting infrastructure projects like retrofitting or rebuilding critical facilities, and developing programs to help residents make their properties more resilient. articles.text: Janet Crandall, a lifelong Piedmont resident, died on January 10. She was 86. Lifelong resident of Piedmont Janet King Crandall passed away at the age of 86 on January 10, 2025. Janet was born in Oakland on July 19, 1938 to Dr. Leroy M. King and Mrs. Dorothy Lossman King from Piedmont and grew up attending Piedmont schools. She was a loving wife, mother, and grandmother. Her friends describe her as outgoing, smart, energetic, and a very kind and supportive friend. Janet met the love of her life, Sheldon Crandall, when they were both 15 and sophomores at Piedmont High School. They had both volunteered to plan and decorate for a welcome dance for the incoming freshman class at the Piedmont Community Hall. Sheldon was up on a ladder attaching streamers and Janet just had to know who this impressive young man was. With a wink and a smile, and with his hard work, he stole her heart. They continued getting to know each other while awaiting a delivery from the Coca-Cola company truck. Janet graduated from Piedmont High School in June 1956 and attended UC Berkeley, where she was a member of the Delta Delta Delta sorority. Shortly after graduation in 1960, Janet and Sheldon were married at Piedmont Community Church. She continued her education at UCSF to become a licensed physical therapist. She practiced initially in San Jose and later in Oakland with Webster Orthopedics. She continued her love of learning throughout her life and was an avid reader. She maintained memberships with the California Physical Therapy Association, Junior League of the East Bay and a number of other smaller groups. Janet spent much of her happiest times in the Plumas National Forest at her family cabin on the Middle Fork of the Feather River, where she became an avid and skilled swimmer. One of her favorite things to do was join friends to ride inner tubes down the river from the Layman Bridge. She taught swimming lessons and performed synchronized swimming shows with her friend Liz Eubanks for guests of the Historic Feather River Inn. She also attended Camp Augusta in Nevada City, where she enjoyed teaching swimming to her younger camp mates. Janet had amazing life experiences, including witnessing “troop trains” traveling on steam trains up and down the Feather River Canyon, off to training and war. During the war, she helped tend to a victory garden with her mother and grandmother. Janet enjoyed being hostess to many groups of family and friends, sharing her love of the rivers, lakes and mountains. She loved the outdoors and animals, even working on the original Save The Whales movement with friends from Berkeley in the 1960s and 70s. Another of her passions was participating in competitive ice skating as a member of the St. Moritz Ice Skating Club at Iceland in Berkeley. She continued her love of the sport, teaching both of her daughters to skate and whenever possible attended or watched national and international skating competitions. Janet was always active in supporting Piedmont schools that her children attended. Eventually three of her six grandchildren also attended Piedmont schools. She remained very close to their grandmother, affectionately calling her Mogo, a nickname that stayed with her until she passed. Janet modeled a lifelong pattern of service to family, friends and community. She was always a very hard worker. She was generous in her support of others, including those she knew well and those she knew little. Janet will be greatly missed by her family and friends. She is survived by her husband of 64 years, Sheldon E. Crandall of Piedmont, son Warren E. Crandall of Grass Valley and daughters Sharon C. Vinn of Danville and Stacy C. Ewing of Piedmont. Additionally, she is survived by her grandchildren Rebecca Crandall of Grass Valley, Michael and Alexander Vinn of Danville and Brett, Scott and Wyatt Ewing of Piedmont and Tiburon. During her final years, she suffered from dementia. She passed away peacefully surrounded by her family. In lieu of flowers the family requests memorial donations be made to Autism Speaks, or any preferred charity. A family celebration of life will be held in the spring. Autism Speaks, P.O. One of the gratifying aspects of writing a wine column for 24 years is witnessing the growth in certain sectors of the wine industry. I recall attending a Rhone Rangers event in the early 2000s. About 25 or 30 wineries poured their wines and discussed then-obscure grape varieties such as Roussanne, Counoise and Mourvedre. The trend toward growing and making Rhone wines in the U.S. was just beginning. Now, years later, hundreds of wineries in California, Oregon and Washington specialize in Rhone varietals. In addition to Rhone Rangers events, the Hospice du Rhone tasting attracts an international crowd of Rhone producers. Over the years, wineries have risen and fallen in quality. However, one constant remains: Tablas Creek, America’s finest producer of Rhone wines, stands above the competition. In 1989, the Perrin family, owners of Chateau Beaucastel in Chateauneuf-du-Pape, France, and American wine importer Robert Haas bought property on a limestone ridge near Paso Robles to make Rhonestyle wines in America. They imported grafts of the vines that made Beaucastel and propagated them in a nursery near the winery. Today, Robert Haas’s son, Jason Haas, manages Tablas Creek. articles.text: Aging is a fact of life and it comes with certain realities. While most of us probably don’t want to picture ourselves eventually needing help with daily activities, Americans turning 65 today have almost a 70 percent chance they will need some type of long-term care during their remaining years.1 As this type of care is not generally covered by private health insurance or Medicare, it’s important to create a strategy to help protect yourself and your family from the financial and emotional impact of a possible long-term care event. retirement and the assets you’ve worked so hard to accumulate. Understanding the various longterm care options available is critical to helping you create a strategy to ensure you have access to the type of care you prefer while protecting your finances. How to prepare for long-term What is long-term care? Long-term care encompasses a variety of services that assist those who can no longer perform everyday activities on their own. These activities, known as activities of daily living (ADLs), include dressing, eating, and bathing. articles.text: Downsizing is a major life transition that comes with emotional and practical challenges. Whether moving to a smaller home, a retirement community or simply decluttering, a strategic approach can make the process smoother and less stressful. Planning ahead and breaking tasks into manageable steps can help you navigate this change with confidence. Where to Begin Downsizing can feel overwhelming due to years of accumulated belongings. To make the process easier, consider these steps: • Assess your needs: Determine the size and type of space you are moving into to decide what furniture and belongings will fit. • Start early: Sorting through items gradually prevents last-minute stress. • Categorize belongings: Create categories such as keep, donate, sell and discard to streamline decision-making. • Seek support: If family members live far away, reach out to friends, neighbors or professional organizers. Managing Your Belongings Deciding what to keep or let go of is one of the biggest challenges. Here are some strategies: • Preserve memories: Take photos or create a memory book for sentimental items that won’t fit in your new space. • Donate or gift: Passing items to family, friends or charities can be a meaningful way to downsize. • Sell unwanted items: Estate sales, online marketplaces and consignment shops can help you sell furniture and valuables. • Use storage wisely: Temporary storage can be an option if you need more time to decide. Emotional Considerations Downsizing isn’t just about logistics — it’s also an emotional journey. To ease the transition: • Focus on the benefits, such as less maintenance and more freedom. • Stay connected with friends and family for emotional support. • Allow yourself time to reminisce while also looking forward to new opportunities. Finding the Right Resources There are many resources available to help make downsizing easier, including: • Senior move managers: Specialists in helping older adults downsize and relocate. • Estate sale services: Companies that assist with selling furniture and valuables. • Professional organizers: Experts in decluttering and space planning. Embracing the Next Chapter While downsizing can be challenging, it is also an opportunity for a fresh start. By planning ahead and seeking support, you can make the process smoother and more positive. Whether preparing for yourself or assisting a loved one, the key is to start early, stay organized and focus on the benefits of this new phase in life. articles.text: Our homes should evolve with us as we age, making today more comfortable while still adding to your home’s value. Fortunately, there are many smart things you can do to make home life easier and increase appeal for future buyers — without breaking the bank. Here are our top suggestions for updates that do just that. Improve Lighting Good lighting isn’t just about aesthetics, it’s essential for visibility and safety. Upgrading to LED fixtures, installing under-cabinet lighting in the kitchen, and adding motion-sensor lights in hallways and entryways can reduce fall risks and make your home feel bright and inviting. Swap Door Handles Round doorknobs can be difficult to grip, especially for those with arthritis. Replacing them with lever-style handles makes opening doors easier, plus choosing a modern finish and durable material brings consistency throughout your home. Secure Flooring Loose rugs can create unnecessary tripping hazards. Securing area rugs with non-slip pads or double-sided tape helps, and eliminating uneven thresholds that can catch toes or walkers makes a big difference. Add Pull-Out Shelving If bending and reaching for items in deep cabinets is becoming difficult, you can make storage more accessible by installing pull-out shelving in kitchen and bathroom cabinets. This also gives a more high-end feel, along with adding soft-close drawer slides to prevent slamming. Install a Smart Home System Voice-activated lights, smart thermostats and video doorbells provide convenience and security — and are modern features that future buyers are looking for. A handyman can help with both installation and setup to ensure everything functions smoothly and you know how to use it. Upgrade Entryways Simple exterior updates like installing brighter porch lights, adding walkway lighting, securing loose railings and adding non-slip treads to outdoor steps are quick ways to boost both curb appeal and safety. The good news is that you don’t need to take on major renovations to make a big impact on your well-being at home. All of these are smart, practical updates that can be done by a trusted handyman or handywoman. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: My husband and I have decided that we want to look at senior facilities, as we are in our late 80s (86 and 89), and are finding our house is just too much to manage. Right now, we can get around and go through our day with little or no help, but we feel the day is coming that we will need assistance. We have no children and have no idea where to even begin. Are there things or sources on the internet to help us begin our search? –Sami, Piedmont Dear Sami: This is such a big issue for those of us nearing the age of needing assistance, both physically, and sometimes in the case of a partner with dementia, mentally. I have helped a few clients in their search, because I went through an extensive search for my mother, when I moved her into an assisted living facility in Florida, and then a year later moved her into memory care in San Francisco so she could be closer to me. I spoke with some friends who are nurses, who gave me a list of questions and issues to address in our tours. Of course, not all facilities have the same care services. Some of them are independent living only, others have independent and assisted living, and some have independent, assisted living, and memory care. And very few have all of those and skilled nursing, which is often for those too ill or infirm for the other types of care. Often though, facilities partner with skilled nursing facilities so the transition is not so overwhelming and traumatic. So, it’s important to know that wherever you move, will serve you as you age. Most places that have at least assisted living care have what they call aging in place, which means that they can provide individual care and allow hospice when the time comes. And many are monthly rent, and some are actual buy ins, like a condo. And all that I visited have a move in fee, that does not go toward rent. I have seen that amount from $5,000-$60,000. When I started the search for my mom, it was all new to me, and the first thing I did was start out with, as you ask about, an internet search. Here are a couple of places that you can start your research, with some cautions and my comments. 1 A Place for Mom (aplaceformom.com) This is where many people start. At no cost to you, this organization assigns an agent who interviews you and suggests some facilities based on the criteria of your needs. This is where I started too, but I wouldn’t recommend this. articles.text: Early Bird passes available now Piedmont Food Fest Mark your calendars for the Piedmont Food Fest, coming to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 19 from 11 a.m. - 4p.m. This annual event builds community by assembling the broadest mix of food, drinks, and performances gathered from around the Bay. Some new additions to the festival include: • Lobster rolls from Maine Lobster (as featured on Food Network), Nepalese momos from Momolicious, Peruvian street food from La Pituca, piping hot pies from Hearth Wood-Fired Pizza, and towering creations from Rock Club Burgers • A special children’s performance in the KidZone by the famed Prescott Circus Theater, a youth circus program that’s worked with local schools since 1984. • An art exhibit on food waste from the Art for Advocacy club from PHS. • An informational booth run by PHS students promoting the Alameda County Food Bank’s efforts to fight food insecurity. Attendees can also enjoy fan favorites such as: • Baos from The Chairman, seafood paella from Lola’s Spanish Cuisine, Japanese fried chicken sandwiches from Aburaya, boba from Tea on Piedmont, empanadas, patacon, and arepas from Crazy Empanadas, sambusas from Swahili Spot • Tastings from Deer Hill Vineyards, Mount Diablo Cider Company, Maker Wine, Blindwood Cider, and P. Herrell Winery • Midway games, sno-cones, crafts, and henna tattoos at the KidZone carnival • Live music from HiiiWAV artist showcase, Oakland Taiko, Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Beloved Little Circus aerialists, and many more! Registration and Early Bird discounts on all-day tastings and KidZone passes (through March only) are available at www.piedmontfoodfest.org.
